metadata.title: Testing Graph Database Systems via Equivalent Query Rewriting
metadata.description: GRev rewrites a graph-database query into many equivalent queries via an Abstract Syntax Graph, finding 22 previously unknown bugs in five graph databases.

two-answers-to-one-question.title: Testing Graph Database Systems via Equivalent Query Rewriting

children.text: (co-first author), Boxi Yu, Hanfei Chen, Pinjia He.
, the 46th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering, Lisbon.
Ask a graph database one question in many equivalent ways; where the answers disagree, there is a bug. GRev found
previously unknown bugs in Neo4j, RedisGraph, MemGraph, TinkerGraph and NebulaGraph: 15 confirmed by developers, 14 in graph data retrieval itself.
The opening example is one of them. On the same graph, RedisGraph counts 7 for the first phrasing and 8 for the second, although both ask for the same pattern (
). No other database and no hand-written expected answer is needed to see the bug: the two answers contradict each other.

parameters.alt: Two equivalent Cypher queries on the same RedisGraph data count 7 and 8.

children.text: Graph databases have no common query language: Neo4j speaks Cypher, TinkerGraph Gremlin, NebulaGraph nGQL. The two families of testers before GRev each work under a condition that leaves graph traversal untested.

Differential testers such as GDsmith and Grand send one query to several databases and compare the answers. That requires databases that share a language, so they test only shared features, and porting them to a new language is extensive engineering; existing research covers at most Cypher and Gremlin.
GDBMeter reuses Ternary Logic Partitioning from relational testing: it splits a
predicate into its true, false and null parts. The traversal in
is never changed, and none of its reported bugs are graph-related.
Neither family targets performance bugs: different engines differ in speed by design, and partitioned sub-queries have no expected timing relation to the original.

parameters.alt: Comparing databases needs a shared query language; partitioning a filter leaves the graph walk unchanged.

children.text: The insight: the meaning of a graph query can live in the paths of a graph. GRev parses a query into an

(ASG): its vertices are the kinds of nodes to retrieve, with their label and property constraints; its edges are the relationships between them. Any set of non-overlapping paths that together cover every edge and constraint is an equivalent query.

picks a random path, removes its edges and a random part of its vertices' constraints, and translates the path back into a query fragment, until the ASG is covered exactly once. Because the ASG is language-independent, a new query language needs only a translator (about 260 lines of Python for Cypher), not new rewrite rules.

children.text: A database cannot predict the shape of the graph before it runs a query, so different path orders are hard to optimise into one plan. The rewrites therefore reach different code, and GRev checks each pair three ways:
the results differ and no exception is raised.
the results differ and an exception is raised (unexpected or missing).
the slower query is at least 5× and at least 1,000 ms slower.
Ten long base queries with 300 rewrites each triggered
distinct query plans in RedisGraph; ten random ones, 178 (Fig. 6). Partitioning yields at most 4 plans per base query, differential testing one per database.
2,394 of 3,000 rewrites of random base queries and all 3,000 of long ones were unique (Fig. 5).
In 12 hours, 1,250,000 test cases on RedisGraph gave 945 bug-triggering ones, one per 1,322 executions, about one a minute.

parameters.alt: Equivalent queries fall into the database and trigger distinct query plans: 1,253 for ten long base queries.

children.text: By type: 12 logic bugs, 3 performance bugs, 4 missing and 3 unexpected exceptions (Table 2). No performance report was rejected as a false alarm.
Most of the bugs are graph-related, a class that partitioning-based testing did not reach: all of GDBMeter's logic bugs came from queries with only a simple

or a returned expression. 9 of the 13 bugs from MemGraph, RedisGraph and TinkerGraph (69%) also reproduce in the older versions that earlier tools tested, so those tools had missed them; the Neo4j bugs involve newer features such as label expressions.

Coverage depends on the system: with the same base-query generator, GRev reached higher instruction and branch coverage than GDsmith on Neo4j; on RedisGraph it matched GDsmith, and GDBMeter's more diverse base queries reached higher coverage.

content.text: one question two ways, on the same data. One phrasing counts seven, the other eight. One of them is wrong.
Testers compare different databases, which only works where they share a query language, or split a query's filter, which never changes how the graph is walked. Bugs in the walk slip past.
's idea: a query is a small graph of what to match. Cover that graph with random paths, each edge used once, and each covering asks the same question in new words.
Each new wording can send the database down a different internal route, so one question exercises many query plans, and every route must reach the same answer.
When two routes disagree, the database has a bug, like seven against eight. Asking the same question many ways,
found 22 previously unknown bugs in five graph databases.
